query: Refractory high-entropy alloys are promising structural materials, but achieving a strong combination of strength and plasticity remains important. What single intervention could improve this strength–plasticity combination? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate reference alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled amount of Ti to the NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy will improve the strength–plasticity combination by enhancing grain boundary cohesion.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory NbMoTaW high-entropy alloy with a primarily BCC structure that exhibits high yield strength but limited plasticity at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Introduce Ti as a minor alloying addition to the NbMoTaW composition (i.e., forming a NbMoTaWTi alloy) compared to the baseline NbMoTaW alloy.
generation.conditions: Process both the baseline and the Ti-doped alloys under identical conditions using mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering; evaluate mechanical properties at room temperature using standard tensile and compressive tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain boundary cohesion induced by Ti addition, which may also help moderate lattice mismatch and promote more uniform dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Ti atoms segregate to grain boundaries and possibly alter the local chemistry, reducing intergranular brittleness and facilitating more effective dislocation motion. This improvement in grain boundary cohesion is expected to enhance ductility while maintaining high strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ti-doped NbMoTaWTi alloy will exhibit an improved ductility (greater plastic strain) at room temperature relative to the baseline alloy, with yield strength remaining at a similar level or being modestly enhanced.
generation.baseline: The original NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy, which shows high strength but poor plasticity at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The positive effect of Ti addition is expected under the specified powder metallurgy route (mechanical alloying and SPS) and evaluated at room temperature; deviations in processing conditions or temperature may alter the balance of strength and plasticity.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Ti concentration and the exact magnitude of the ductility improvement are uncertain and will depend on detailed processing parameters and compositional tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys: one baseline NbMoTaW and one Ti-doped NbMoTaWTi alloy, using identical mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering conditions. Subject both alloys to room-temperature tensile and compressive tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in ductility (plastic strain) compared to the baseline, or if its yield strength is substantially reduced, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years []. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co []. First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [,]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 []. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [] and yield strength σ0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [].
